title: Database index
short: A sorted lookup list so the database skips the full scan.
what: An index is an extra sorted structure the database keeps for one column, with a pointer from each value to its row. Instead of reading every row, the database searches the sorted index in a few steps. Real databases use a B-tree, a wide sorted tree, so even a billion rows take only 3 or 4 disk reads.
analogy: The index at the back of a textbook. To find 'photosynthesis' you don't read every page; you look it up alphabetically and jump to page 212.

frames.label: users table (row order)
frames.say: A users table, stored in signup order. You ask for the user named lea. There is no index yet.

frames.label: users table (row order)
frames.say: With no index, the database reads rows one by one: tom, ana, zoe, kim. None of them is lea.

frames.label: users table (row order)
frames.say: Row 7 is lea. But names aren't unique, so it can't stop here. Another lea could be further down.

frames.label: users table (row order)
frames.say: 10 reads for 10 rows: a full table scan. With 10 million users, that's 10 million reads and seconds per query.

frames.label: index on name (sorted)
frames.say: CREATE INDEX builds a sorted copy of the name column. Each entry keeps a pointer to its row, like lea -> row 7.

frames.label: index on name (sorted)
frames.say: Search it like a phone book. The middle entry is kim. lea comes after kim, so the whole left half is skipped.

frames.label: index on name (sorted)
frames.say: The middle of what's left is sam. lea comes before sam, so the right part goes too.

frames.label: index on name (sorted)
frames.say: Next is lea: found in 3 steps, then jump to row 7. For 10 million rows it's about 24 steps instead of 10 million reads.

when: A query is slow and filters on one column
You look rows up by email, username or id
You sort or filter by a range, like dates
python:
import bisect, math
names = ["tom", "ana", "zoe", "kim", "bob", "eve", "sam", "lea", "max", "ivy"]

reads = 0
for row, name in enumerate(names):          # no index: read every row
    reads += 1
    if name == "lea":
        found = row
print("full scan: row", found, "after", reads, "reads")

index = sorted((name, row) for row, name in enumerate(names))   # CREATE INDEX
i = bisect.bisect_left(index, ("lea",))     # binary search in the sorted index
print("index: row", index[i][1])
print("10 million rows:", math.ceil(math.log2(10_000_000)), "steps instead of 10,000,000 reads")
output:
full scan: row 7 after 10 reads
index: row 7
10 million rows: 24 steps instead of 10,000,000 reads
cost: a bit slower: every index changes too
an extra copy of the column per index
watch: Every index slows writes and uses disk; index the columns you search by, not all of them.
An index on (last_name, first_name) helps searches by last_name, but not by first_name alone.
Wrapping the column in a function, like LOWER(name), can stop the index from being used.
